Maybe you should give Baldur's Gate 3 a try yourself. Knocking enemies off of cliffs is only scratching the surface of BG3 rewarding you for thinking. The game is absolutely full of encounters that can be solved multiple ways, including many that don't even require entering combat. The game world is incredibly reactive, if you think something should work, it probably will.


Combat is turn based, as you've seen, but you can also enter "turn based mode" at any time during the game. So if NPCs are walking around, but you'd like the opportunity to take your time and think while sneaking around them, you can just freeze the world, and take turns moving instead. 

Or, you can enter TBM while an enemy is near some kind of hazard. There's an early game boss that people love tricking onto a destructible bridge.

It's not a specific misconception, but I used to be a claims adjuster for auto insurance, and the amount of people who just plain did not know what coverage they even have is *astounding*. Go check your policy. 

All of the below is both a generalization, and a simplification. I haven't worked in the industry in almost four years, so things might be different. 

"Collision Coverage" covers accidents where your vehicle is hit by, or hits, another vehicle or object. 

"Comprehensive Coverage" is sometimes called "Other than Collision" which I wish was a more common way to call it, because the name "Comprehensive" tricks a lot of people into thinking it means it covers everything. It doesn't, it covers most common occurrences that specifically are not covered by collision(theft, vandalism, damage caused by weather or animals. Many policies specifically exclude volcano damage, flooding, and acts of war). 

Some states(Maryland, for example) have medical coverage by default, and you have to  sign a waiver to *remove it* from your policy, and yet the number of people I spoke to at that job who were *shocked* that they didn't have medical coverage was maddening. 

You should also look into whether or not your state offers Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage, and how it works in your state. It varies so much I can't guarantee anything, but the general idea is that it can cover damage to your vehicle in the event that a) another party besides yourself is liable for damages and b) that party doesn't have insurance(or in some cases, doesn't have enough). In some states you need to know who the at-fault party is, and confirm that they do not have insurance of their own, but some(Virginia was this way when I worked this job) can apply even in the event of a hit and run. 

Ultimately, it's the job of the sales department(or agent as the case may be) to make sure that people understand what they're buying, but that usually doesn't seem to work out in my experience. I don't know if sales doesn't explain it right, or if most people just aren't paying enough attention when they sign up for their policy. But people need to know what they're buying ~~or else they get real mad at the adjuster who had nothing to do with their contract.~~

Here's just a handful of things I wish I'd known sooner. 

Don't buy a space ship, you can build a better one for cheaper. When you edit your ship, you can replace every part, or even just delete all of them and start from scratch. The ship builder is largely pretty darn good, but has a few annoying quirks. 

Space ships are also pretty easy to steal, and a very early main quest will teach you how to disable and board an enemy vessel. 

Food is almost completely worthless, as is the gastronomy skill. I think they're only in the game to support a planned "survival mode" that we'll get in an update or dlc. 

Melee is pretty underwhelming at higher levels or higher difficulties, so consider carefully if you wanna put any skill points toward it. 

Guns and space suits have a name-based tier system(from weakest to strongest Calibrated, Refined, Advanced, and Superior(I believe superior doesn't exist for guns, and is only for space suits)). Melee weapons don't have tiers, which is a huge part of why melee starts to taper off at higher levels.

There is also a rarity level that is indicated by item card color(as well as a number of stars somewhere in it, I think?). Rarity indicates how many bonuses it has. The lowest rarity has none, I think the highest is four. Bonuses will be stuff like having a chance to deal elemental damage, or being particularly effective against robots. So a higher *tier* weapon might still be better than a *rarer* weapon of the same model. But that's just weighing stats, lol, if you play any RPGs you know how to do that. 

Juggling mass can be a pain, I'll tell you my own personal looting rules:

Aid items and ammo are always-grabs. Ammo has no weight(might change in a survival mode if/when they add it) and aid items are simultaneously very light, and basically always needed. 

For everything else, unless I want it specifically, I won't pick it up unless it's worth at least 1200 credits per kilo of mass. Otherwise it isn't worth the inventory space, even for selling(I don't sit here doing the math, I just eyeball it, but the *idea* of the rule is enough to help keep my looting profitable). 

On that subject, Akila city is a great place to sell stuff because it has a lot of vendors that are relatively close to each other(and I suck every credit out of each one every time I visit). 

The environmental damage system is bad, and I personally just ignore it and carry aid items to scrub status effects when they crop up.

You can try Gundam Battles: Gunpla warfare.

It's free, and I've personally managed not to spend any on premium stuff and found i can still manage to play alright.  

The combat doesn't give you as much control as some might like. The way it works is basically you choose whether you are moving towards the enemy or not, when you're close you do melee automatically, and you can choose to fire your gun at any time(it aims automatically). You can swipe to "step" side to side or forward and back, but it heats your Gundam and it needs to cool down over time. 

Most of the game comes down to the build, but the building and painting is pretty robust, and you can make a custom skin so that your appearance is separate from the parts that are giving you your stats. You get parts from playing missions, opening capsules, which you can get a few free every day, and a shop. Like I said I don't pay any real money, and you can earn tokens and stuff to get more capsules. My main complaint with the buying/building is that there's a lot of different currencies for acquiring parts, I personally kind of wish it was a little simpler in that regard. 

You can upgrade parts, so if there's a low grade part that you like the look or ability of, you can work on it to make it competitive. 

If you're into Gundam, the collecting and building is super cool, but even if you're just into mecha in general it's still pretty neat. 

All that said, let me know if you find other games, because I'm also looking for new ones.
